en: When a husband dies, to his wife
Her birth family becomes near;
Flee toward Temirkhan!
When you reach Temirkhan,
Semetey in your arms—
Have his little twig trimmed;
Tell him then
The rite in which he may trust.
When he reaches twelve,
Put a musket in his hand.
Cherish the boy,
Show him Talas again.
If my spirit is present,
I shall meet him on the road;
Upon the orphan beset with troubles
I shall keep one eye.
Leopard Bakai, my khan and friend,
Do not camp along the river;
As though the goshawk, King Manas,
Were still alive, do not behave!
If you behave as though I lived,
With eyes reddened like a raven's,
Trailing your white beard,
Let them not call you wretched Bakai;
Let your poor life not end that day!
When the khan dies, the elder
Camps along the steep bank.
Do not approach a great gathering;
When his lord dies, the elder
Stays close to the camels.
Tend the camels, uncle;
Zhelmayaan and Bozbuura,
Hang amulets around their necks.
‘A keepsake from my khan,’ say,
And tend the orphan's camels!
Perish with your feast!
Do not approach a gathering.
If the neighboring households quarrel,
Do not add your provocation;
Above all, leopard Bakai,
Do not go among them.
Keep your horse well saddled;
‘My generous friend has died,’ say,
And at the proper time lament and recite the Quran.
Go up into the hills and pause;
‘My generous Manas has died,’ say.
If you heed my words,
Go on lamenting me aloud!
Grasp the lance and turn it;
Until my dear life goes beyond,
To give your counsel to those remaining,
Watch beside me, Bakai!
Khan Koshoi of the Katagan—
Tell him to stand at my funeral prayer.
Eleman's brave Töshtük—
Tell him to render me faithful service.
Urumkhan's Kökbörü—
Tell him to scatter his wealth.
Karacha's Saykal—
Tell her to tear her face bloody.
The forty holy men of Andijan—
I have done them harm;
Tell them to receive my offerings for absolution!
When my dear life dies,
Bakai, my mountain horses number nine thousand;
Set aside a thousand bays for absolution.
My camels in the hills number six thousand;
When my noble life departs,
Set aside a thousand of my camels.
Bakai, my friend, I drank spirits;
See that you lift that burden from my neck.
Will it save my poor soul
From the divorce oath upon my neck?
See that you save my poor soul
From adultery's sin and torment.
I slaughtered every khan's commanders;
I consumed the livestock of every man.
I laid great torment upon the people;
I plundered much of their gold.
Those who truly heeded my words,
I subdued with my words.
The ignorant who would not heed,
I beat until they begged.
When I reached twelve,
I destroyed a royal camp and took booty.
When I reached thirteen,
I attacked a people with a royal court.
I bloodied my sword's point;
I reduced every place I met to dust.
I tethered my steeds across the way.
Whoever provoked me,
I slew without looking back.
Sated with blood, I grew hardened.
Bringing strife upon the earth,
I was called leopard Manas.
I seized those who opposed me;
Whoever provoked me,
I seized and slew.
Whoever challenged my wrath,
I caught between my molars and chewed.
I became a man of sacred power;
I was khan upon the earth for forty-two years.
With my horse fattened, I grew strong.
I was alone; I became forty.
I gathered harriers and made them hawks;
I gathered slaves and made them a people.
I gathered gold and made it common as stone.
Over this people standing here,
I made the wandering people leaders.
At first I meant to stay;
Now I am to pass away, you see,
At fifty-two years of age.
Drawing blood and laying men low,
In the mire of Beijing itself,
While I was saying prayers,
Alöökö's Kongurbay
Had me speared from behind.
The steel point struck with a thud,
Broke off in my spine;
The wound's mouth closed tight,
But inside it festered and brought turmoil.”
The hero's appointed end
Had drawn near.
That dear sister-in-law Kanykey,
Her sacred power truly gone,
That her blood-shedding hero had come back ill,
Had failed to recognize then.
Khan Bakai and Kanykey
Walked around him, looking anxiously;
Unable to collect themselves,
That noble sister-in-law Kanykey,
For six calves and four yearling colts,
Had bought a white-steel blade.
As the hero's strength failed,
She aimed directly at the wound
And touched its mouth with it.
That moving piece of steel,
Your sister-in-law reached in her hand
And pulled it out.
The steel left in his bone
Had worked its way onward;
The living marrow in his backbone
Had rotted away completely.
His threadlike mustache trailed;
What a grievous illness, a dreadful affair!
That one whose trot the wind could not match,
Whose walk no beast could match,
The broad-humped black camel,
With a golden halter on its head,
Khan Manas's Zhelmayaan,
They made kneel beside him.
When Akkula fell to a bullet,
Manas, heavy as lead,
It had borne without faltering.
Brave Kongurbay and countless governors,
When your fierce-maned hero Manas
Pursued them down the slopes,
Without betraying its youth,
It turned its neck like a stag.
When slaughter fell upon the Chinese,
If a man-high ditch appeared,
It raced across without delay.
Its back was high, its saddle low;
Sent into hills, it would not flag.
Karacha's Saykal,
After their clash, had given the roan horse;
Illustrious Saykal
Had given the roan horse as a gift.
They tethered it close before the hero.
Tethered, it would not stand still;
Released, it would not graze.
Though a beast, it was a living soul;
It had no tongue to speak then,
And kept only mourning.
Unable to stand her anguished weeping,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
With Argynkhan's Ajybai
Took counsel.
Then from her dear quail-like eyes
Tears fell separately;
From her dear currant-like eyes
Tears flowed a whip-length.
Argynkhan's Ajybai—
She spoke her grief to him:
“Dear Ajy, white-headed horses in the hills,
Thoroughbreds and mighty steeds together;
The one to bring word to the world,
Our son left behind, is young.
Those who should grieve for the Generous One,
His elder and younger brothers, are all enemies.
To prepare his funeral properly,
The Argyn and Kyrgyz themselves foremost,
To spread great tidings to the world,
To gather the khans here,
Our son left behind, is young.
Dear Ajy, the hawthorn-hafted battle-axe—
Who will haft it without letting it twist?
If the mountain-like hero closes his eyes,
Who will lead this without disorder?
The black-edged battle-axe—
Who will take it up and hold it?
If my khan closes his eyes,
The dear handful of people—
Who will know how to spare them grief?
My elder brother, like a prophet,
I am torn apart; join me again!
Dear Ajy, I am about to scatter; gather me!
I am about to go out; rekindle me!
Dear Ajy, I am about to die; bring me to life!
Knowing the tongues of sixty tribes,
My uncle, swiftest among men,
Heed the words of this unfortunate woman.
Forty days' journey away,
Among the people called Urum,
Lives Kökbörü, Urumkhan's son.
Send word to our family friend;
Dear Ajy, go as a swift messenger.
Dear Ajy, the seven giants upon the earth—
Let us bury the hero without strife;
Let us act of our own free will.
Hero, go and gather them!
To the four corners of the world,
Uncle, send word to each.
If a khan is close to your lord,
Uncle, gather every one.
To the five corners of Medina,
Send word to each appointed place.
If a khan is a steadfast friend of Manas,
Hero, gather him here!
To the khans who have been enemies,
Dear Ajy, do not turn aside to bring word.
If a harsh man confronts you,
Attacking with a clamor, dear Ajy,
The one who would strike fiercely at a people,
Dear Ajy, your commanding lion Manas is gone.
Dear Ajy, return without taking the Chet-Kayt road;
Let your widow suffer no affliction.
Dear Ajy, return no later than the seventh day!
Return without ranging over the mountain pass;
Dear Ajy, while your Generous One lies thus,
Without making us suffer,
Dear Ajy, return no later than six days!
If your friend remains unburied,
Let the enemies intent on mischief
Not assemble,
Seeking vengeance on the corpse,
Dragging it along the road,
Abandoning it to dogs in a day of ruin!
Let the witless, ignorant people
Not take vengeance thus!
Dear Ajy, listen now to my words.
Do not leave behind in Alay
Your wolf, Töshtük.
Never forget, I beg you,
Your lion, leopard Koshoi.
Set at the front, he brings good fortune;
